name: Open Source

claims.claim_text: Open source is an ecosystem rather than a technology, and treating it as only a technical artefact is the mistake newcomers most often make. The code is the smaller half of what a project is.
claims.quote_verbatim: They think of open source as a technology and it's really not
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: The practical form of engaging with that ecosystem is physical: conferences, user groups and hackerspaces. The people who wrote widely used projects are directly accessible in a way that authors inside a corporation never are, so you can end up talking with them without realising who they are.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually go up there and shake hands with the person who wrote whatever it is
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Community norms run stricter than the licence and cover things the licence deliberately does not. The legal text permits essentially everything, so the expectation that you credit and interoperate with the original author exists only as an unwritten rule.
claims.quote_verbatim: all those hardware licenses say you're legally allowed to do all this. End of story.
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Large volunteer projects converge on conventional structure. One that began deliberately loose and emergent ended up with roles, responsibilities, team leads, interviews before people join, version control and code review, arriving at something resembling a corporate organisation chart.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have, you know, roles and responsibilities and team leads
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: The one thing that does not transfer from a company is coercion. Volunteers need more careful and attentive management than employees, not less, because an unhappy volunteer simply stops showing up.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they're not happy, they'll leave
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: The underlying claim is that open source is fundamentally a social arrangement: pulling together a team and creating an architecture of participation, with the technical output following from that rather than the other way round.
claims.quote_verbatim: open source is all about the social factors
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Running a hardware project with the full apparatus of a software project, public repositories, wikis, mailing lists and chat channels, is what converts users into contributors. The tooling is not incidental; it is what makes participation possible at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the things that people commonly do to execute and support open source software projects, I do with my open source hardware projects
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: That apparatus doubles as a hiring pipeline. One project's entire recruiting method was taking volunteers already known to do good work and offering them paid contract work once funding existed.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's my only recruiting method really is just taking volunteers
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Paying contributors by milestone rather than by time shifts the estimation risk onto them, which works because the people taking that risk are contributing partly for reasons unrelated to the money.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of my contracts that I have out there are, are for specific milestones
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: The naive assumption worth discarding early is that declaring a project open will summon contributors. People's time is constrained, and openness on its own changes nothing about that.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, well I'll just say it's open and people will come
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: Hiring from your own project forum works unusually well: candidates already know the work inside out because everything is public, you have seen what they can do before making an offer, and there is nothing to train them on.
claims.quote_verbatim: we try to hire people out of our forum
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: The concrete way to unblock contribution is to write the work down publicly. Posting an issue listing every repository that needs the same change lets people who offered help simply start checking items off, which is far more effective than an open invitation.
claims.quote_verbatim: I wrote up a GitHub issue on it
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Shawcroft

claims.claim_text: The obligation that comes with accepting help is to respect that contributors are giving their own time and to let them get over the hurdles they hit at their own pace. Treating volunteer effort as free labour destroys the supply of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: respect that they're giving you their time
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Shawcroft

claims.claim_text: A maintainer transition can be handled deliberately rather than by collapse. When one project's long-serving maintainer stepped back, the project leader recruited a group of officers given enough explicit authority to drive the areas they cared about.
claims.quote_verbatim: blessed autonomy
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: The structural gap that made those appointments necessary is a common one: most contributions come from people who need one specific change for their work or research and then return to their day jobs, leaving few people working on the underlying architecture or reviewing anyone else's contributions.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll implement the change and and then uh go back to their day jobs
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: Governing a distributed volunteer project carries every conflict a company has, between developers, users and support, with the additional constraint that nobody can be paid and the team is entirely remote.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're not going to pay anyone
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: Open projects have remarkably poor data on who uses them. The perverse consequence is that poor documentation is informative: it generates questions, and the questions reveal who is actually using the work and how deeply they have got into it.
claims.quote_verbatim: usually have a little bit better data. If your documentation is very poor
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: In the absence of better data, repository watchers and stars serve as a crude floor on the interested population rather than a measure of use.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's like your floor
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: The recurring disappointment for users is that a project with a proper licence and a tidy repository frequently does not build. Missing files or an incomplete release mean nobody has run it successfully since the author last did.
claims.quote_verbatim: The author forgot to add a couple of files
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: That failure is silent and self-reinforcing. Rather than reporting the problem, the user gives up and writes their own version, so the defect stays in place and the effort is duplicated.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of like giving feedback, it's like, ah, screw this. I'll do it myself
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: A persistent misconception is that free to use implies nobody spent time building it and nobody is spending time maintaining it. Maintainers are frequently doing the work at night, unpaid, for their own reasons.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of people think that if something is open source, it means it should be free
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Vendor library licences can be incompatible with open projects through discriminatory clauses, such as forbidding use of a header on anyone else's hardware. That single restriction is enough to force a complete reimplementation.
claims.quote_verbatim: this clause of being discriminatory, quote unquote, is incompatible with open source licenses
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: The other half of the problem is the absence of a return path. Finding bugs in a vendor library is useless if there is no mechanism to submit the fix, so every user repairs the same defects privately and forever.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no good way of contributing changes and fixes to the ST libraries back
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Treat a promise to open something later as equivalent to closed. The waiting usually does not end, and the incentive to withhold until shipping is real enough that the promise should carry no weight in your decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: if somebody says something will be open source in the future, that's the same as saying it's closed source
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: Openness is uneven even among its advocates. Research presented at an open conference is routinely published in closed journals, and documentation frequently is not published at all, which is why the useful question is how open your source actually is rather than whether it is open.
claims.quote_verbatim: how open is your source
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: People arrive at open source for genuinely incompatible reasons, political, commercial and practical, and coalesce around the term while expecting different things from it. Disagreements about what openness requires usually trace back to that.
claims.quote_verbatim: People have different reasons to be open and different things that they're expecting to get as a result of being open
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: There is a wrong kind of openness: publishing your own protocol and specification while having invented it from scratch instead of adopting an existing open approach. It multiplies incompatible standards under an open banner and leaves integration harder than before.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like a right kind of openness to approaching a problem
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: The reason that keeps happening is commercial rather than technical. It rarely makes business sense for a large vendor to join someone else's ecosystem when they need to sell a complete solution, so the decision is made by marketing even where the engineers would prefer interoperation.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a marketing decision to brand and try and sell that as a solution
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: Non-disclosure agreements are the concrete barrier openness removes. Many engineers will refuse a part outright if the datasheet requires signing an NDA, regardless of how cheap or good the part is.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of engineers I know will not touch a device if you have to sign the NDA to get the data sheet
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: The standard advice for someone with no professional experience is to contribute to an open project, because it supplies what a first job would: someone architecting the design, mentors who have to help you, grunt work that teaches the flow, and a great deal of self-directed learning.
claims.quote_verbatim: get involved in an open source project
claims.episode_title: Open Orbific Oratiuncle

claims.claim_text: From the hiring side the same point is stated bluntly: demonstrated initiative on a public project is what a manager is actually looking for, and candidates who claim no experience while having done nothing publicly are choosing that position.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to hire the next guy who walks in the door that says he's done that
claims.episode_title: Ludibrious Luxating Layout

claims.claim_text: The opportunity for a newcomer is in neglected projects. Many languish because nobody is working on them, so someone with time and moderate skill can contribute most of the remaining effort and have that be genuinely valuable.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can come along and, woof, can contribute most of the effort to it
claims.episode_title: Ludibrious Luxating Layout

claims.claim_text: Reading other people's published work is a route into the profession itself. One practitioner learned how things worked from open projects, which is what made it possible to write his own software and get a paid programming job as a teenager.
claims.quote_verbatim: I learned from other open source projects, how things worked
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Samy Kamkar

claims.claim_text: Publishing functions as a defence rather than a giveaway. An idea that is published enters the prior art, so it cannot later be patented and used against you, which makes publication the cheapest available protection for an idea you cannot afford to patent.
claims.quote_verbatim: the best defense for the future is to publish everything
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and Self Publishing

claims.claim_text: Before open licences existed the way to open a design was to publish a full construction article in a hobbyist magazine. The practice long predates the terminology, which is worth remembering when the field is described as new.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's how you opened your project, was to publish it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and Self Publishing

claims.claim_text: Ready-made licences are what made the modern practice viable at scale. Previously you either wrote your own terms or paid a lawyer thousands of dollars, and being able to pick a defensible licence off the shelf is arguably the precondition for the whole field.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't think the open source hardware industry would exist if those licenses didn't exist
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cultural Differences

claims.claim_text: A platform hosting open designs can reasonably decline to police licences at all: let users declare whichever licence they want, but neither track nor enforce it, on the grounds that tracking derivation across forks is an impossible problem and enforcement is not the business you are in.
claims.quote_verbatim: we don't want to be like, uh, IP lawyers
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: The default-public model inverts the usual arrangement: everything a user creates is open unless they pay for privacy, which makes openness the path of least resistance rather than a deliberate act.
claims.quote_verbatim: default to community, everything's open source
claims.episode_title: 3D Printed Shark Jumps - Edifying Edison's Energy

claims.claim_text: An aggregator that requires sign-up or payment before releasing the source of a contributed project is gating something its author gave away. Adding value with better presentation is defensible; withholding the source behind a login is a different act.
claims.quote_verbatim: somebody's gone to the effort to submit their open source project to this site
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Analog Components, First Person Flying and Idea Ownership

claims.claim_text: A necessary corrective to absolutism: open source is one model among several rather than the only legitimate one, and something challenging it is not automatically wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: Open source is just one model
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: Splitting hardware and software between two people creates a support asymmetry that can persist for years. In one case the hardware author fielded every support query for a decade while the software author was largely insulated from them.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had to answer all the support queries for the hardware
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: The argument that persuaded one designer not to open a product was support load rather than copying: publishing the firmware means fielding requests about every unofficial modification anyone makes, and those arrive at the original vendor regardless of who caused them.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'll get support requests for every tin pot thing
claims.episode_title: Re-scoping the problem

claims.claim_text: The marketing effect of openness is real even when nobody exercises it. Labelling a product open and publishing the firmware sells additional units because buyers value the option, and most of them never modify anything.
claims.quote_verbatim: saying it's open source, here's the firmware would probably sell a few more units
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Don't Turn It On, Don't Take It Apart

claims.claim_text: The pragmatic case for publishing the schematic specifically is that it protects nothing to withhold it. Anyone sufficiently motivated can reverse engineer a schematic in a day, so the only thing secrecy costs is the goodwill of the people who wanted it.
claims.quote_verbatim: anyone can reverse engineer the schematic in a day
claims.episode_title: Don't Turn It On, Don't Take It Apart

claims.claim_text: When everything is published, competitive advantage moves to what cannot be copied from a file: volume, manufacturing efficiency and how the business is run. That is why opening a design costs less than it appears to.
claims.quote_verbatim: the competitive advantage is not the knowledge contained within
claims.episode_title: Tesla, Checklists and Bullies - Emerging External Eupsychics

claims.claim_text: The reciprocity claim from decades of practice is that publishing details and helping people returns more than it costs. Practitioners trained to patent everything and keep it secret consistently fail to see how that could be true.
claims.quote_verbatim: I get back a lot more than I put out there
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: The characteristic waste in hardware is starting from scratch, or privately modifying something that already worked without contributing the improvement back, so the original never improves and the next person repeats the work.
claims.quote_verbatim: the amount of time people like start from scratch
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: A published project should state the constraints behind its costs. Someone comparing their own bill of materials against a project funded from a well-paid job needs that context, and hiding it makes the comparison misleading.
claims.quote_verbatim: here is the constraints that led to that
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: The collaboration openness enables is concrete rather than abstract: firmware developed for one project running on somebody else's board, with each side building on work the other inspired, across organisational boundaries that would otherwise prevent it entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: he's able to benefit from the, um, expertise and, um, code and all the stuff we've done
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: The unglamorous reality behind some open ecosystems is that early community work ran on a leaked vendor toolchain rather than on anything the vendor published. The community formed before the openness did.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was a leaked SDK
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeroen Domburg (Sprite_tm)

claims.claim_text: Community contribution converts into employment through a recognisable path: writing the missing piece a vendor had on its roadmap but no time for, out of self-interest, led to the vendor's chief executive making contact and eventually to a job.
claims.quote_verbatim: I got a mail from the CEO of Espressif
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeroen Domburg (Sprite_tm)

claims.claim_text: The reason for initially declining payment for that work is worth understanding: being paid converts a voluntary interest into an obligation to keep developing something you may stop caring about, which is a real cost to the contributor.
claims.quote_verbatim: then I all of a sudden need to develop this in order to, you know, uh, be worth my money
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeroen Domburg (Sprite_tm)

claims.claim_text: Open projects attract adaptations their authors never planned. A stenography system published openly drew ports and new theories for other languages simply because people could ask questions and then build, which a closed project forecloses entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's one of the benefits of the open center project because it's open source people just ask questions
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: Opening a design at the end of its commercial life ensures its survival and lets users investigate it, which matters because the alternative is that the work disappears with the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: That it will ensure the survival of it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Longevity is a legitimate purchase criterion alongside likelihood of success. For a connected product, whether a community-supported open alternative exists determines whether the device still works when the vendor's service goes away.
claims.quote_verbatim: will there be, will there be an open source alternative that is actually supported by the community
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: The same reasoning applies to development tools: choosing an established open toolchain over a vendor environment costs more effort up front and buys the assurance that it will still exist later, which is a trade worth making deliberately rather than by default.
claims.quote_verbatim: should you go with more like a GCC tool chain because you know that it's always going to be there
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: A counterweight on formality from someone who ships open designs commercially: putting the files out freely with no binding agreement is enough, people will find them, and open communities can become unhelpfully particular about certification and labelling.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they put their stuff out there and it's free and easy to get ahold of, and there's no binding license agreement, you know, I think that's enough
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: The scale limit specific to hardware is collaborative rather than legal. Nothing exists on the scale of a large collaborative software project, because a single board with more than three or four designers working on it fragments rather than converges.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get more than three or four designers on it and it's just going to splinter
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: A standing risk in open tooling is loss of focus. A project with many contributors can drift toward being a jack of all trades, where one person with a clear idea would have produced a sharper tool for the specific job you need it for.
claims.quote_verbatim: too many cooks spoil the broth
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: HP, IEEE, and Human Interface

Scope note: licensing mechanics, clone economics, open hardware business models and open silicon are covered by the sibling open-source-hardware article, and licence types, open-core and maintainer economics by open-source-software; this packet deliberately takes the community, governance, contribution and definitional angles.
